title: Maimonides’ Negative Theology — knowing God by removing error
when: Developed in the late 12th century; Maimonides completed the Guide of the Perplexed around 1190. Its ideas draw on older Greek and Islamic philosophy.
people: Moses Maimonides (1138–1204); earlier influences included Aristotle and Islamic philosophers such as al-Farabi and Avicenna.
origin: Medieval Jewish philosophy in the Islamicate world. Maimonides was born in Córdoba and wrote the Guide in Judeo-Arabic after settling in Egypt.
idea: Maimonides argues that ordinary positive descriptions of God—wise, powerful, or merciful, for example—risk treating human qualities as if they belonged to God in the same way. They can also make the utterly unified God seem composed of distinct properties. Instead, we can state what God is not: not a body, not changing, not limited. Such denials do not reveal God’s essence; they correct mistaken pictures and narrow the field of what can responsibly be claimed. Biblical language about God’s hands or emotions therefore needs figurative interpretation. Descriptions of divine actions may tell us about effects in the world without defining God’s inner nature.
relevance: The view is a striking lesson in intellectual humility: fluency about a subject is not the same as understanding it. It also gives religious thinkers a way to honor language’s limits without treating all talk about God as meaningless. Its challenge remains live wherever people mistake familiar metaphors for literal explanations.
